# Algorithm (exact step-by-step procedure) (`algorithm_concept`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/computing.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Computing, control & information theory (`computing`)
- Deps: helped by arabic_numerals, symbolic_algebra, formal_logic
- Core idea: An algorithm is a finite list of exact instructions that a person or machine can follow without understanding or judgement, and that always ends with the answer, for every input of its kind and not just one example. Classic case: for non-negative integers a and b, at least one positive, repeatedly replace (a, b) with (b, the remainder of a divided by b) while b is positive. When b is zero, a is the greatest common divisor. Its parts are steps in sequence, decisions (if this, then that) and repetition until a condition holds. Methods differ enormously in the number of steps: finding a name in a sorted list of a million by halving takes 20 comparisons, by reading through takes up to a million.
- Pitfalls:
  - Giving a worked example instead of a rule that covers every case, including zero, equal numbers and empty lists
  - Leaving steps that need judgement, such as 'choose a suitable number'
  - No guarantee that the procedure stops
  - Saying that al-Khwarizmi invented algorithms; the word comes from his name, but written procedures are two and a half thousand years older
- History: mesopotamia: c. 1800–1600 BC – Old Babylonian tablets give general step-by-step procedures for reciprocals, square roots and quadratic problems; egypt: c. 1550 BC – Rhind papyrus (copy of an older text): multiplication and division by doubling and halving; greece: c. 300 BC – Euclid's Elements VII, largest common divisor; 3rd c. BC sieve of Eratosthenes; china: c. 1st c. AD – Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art: elimination for systems of linear equations, root extraction; india: 499 – Aryabhata's kuttaka (pulveriser) for indeterminate equations; islamic: c. 825 – al-Khwarizmi's book on calculation with Indian numerals; its Latin version (Algoritmi de numero Indorum) gives the word; europe: 1843 – Ada Lovelace's table for computing Bernoulli numbers on Babbage's engine; 1936 Turing and Church give the exact definition
- Read:
  - Donald E. Knuth, Ancient Babylonian Algorithms, Communications of the ACM 15 (1972)
  - Jean-Luc Chabert (ed.), A History of Algorithms: From the Pebble to the Microchip (1999)
  - Donald E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, vol. 1: Fundamental Algorithms (1968)
